record.original_question: Give a provable randomized algorithm for backward error diagonalization or Schur form with runtime $O(n^3 ^c(n/delta))$ that only uses $O( (n/delta))$ bits of precision.

evidence.quote: Give a provable randomized algorithm for backward error diagonalization or Schur form with runtime $O(n^3\log^c(n/\delta))$ that only uses $O(\log(n/\delta))$ bits of precision.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ and let $\delta\in(0,1)$. A backward-error diagonalization (resp. Schur form) of $A$ to accuracy $\delta$ is the computation of matrices $V,D$ (resp. $Q,T$) such that
$$\|A - VDV^{-1}\|\le \delta\|A\| \quad\text{(resp. } \|A - QTQ^{*}\|\le \delta\|A\|\text{)},$$
where $D$ is diagonal (resp. $T$ is upper triangular) and, in the Schur case, $Q$ is unitary. The arithmetic is performed in floating-point with $b$ bits of mantissa precision; the runtime is measured in bit operations (or, equivalently, arithmetic operations on $b$-bit numbers).

Construct a provable randomized algorithm that, given any $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ with $\|A\|\le 1$ and any $\delta\in(0,1)$, with high probability outputs a backward-error diagonalization or Schur form of $A$ to accuracy $\delta$, satisfying both of the following:
1. The total runtime is $O\!\bigl(n^{3}\log^{c}(n/\delta)\bigr)$ arithmetic operations for some absolute constant $c\ge 0$.
2. The algorithm uses only $O(\log(n/\delta))$ bits of precision throughout.

Equivalently, exhibit such an algorithm or prove that no such algorithm exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The best known provable randomized backward-error diagonalization algorithm (Banks–Garza-Vargas–Kulkarni–Srivastava, "Pseudospectral Shattering" / "The Complexity of Diagonalization", STOC 2023) achieves runtime O(T_MM(n) log^c(n/δ)) using O(log^c(n/δ)) bits of precision (polylogarithmic, not logarithmic). Achieving the n^3 polylog runtime together with only O(log(n/δ)) bits of precision remains an open problem; recent works (e.g. randomized normal-matrix diagonalization, 2024–2025) make partial progress for structured cases but do not resolve the general question.

status_evidence.title: The Complexity of Diagonalization
status_evidence.snippet: In the finite arithmetic backward error setting the key input comes from random matrix theory... uses O*(log^c(n/δ)) bits of precision.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art uses polylog(n/δ) bits, not log(n/δ); reducing to log(n/δ) bits is not achieved.

status_evidence.title: A simple, randomized algorithm for diagonalizing normal matrices
status_evidence.snippet: A simple numerical method that diagonalizes a complex normal matrix via random Hermitian combination.
status_evidence.claim: Recent partial progress for normal matrices, not the general non-normal case.

status_evidence.title: Fast Linear Algebra is Stable
status_evidence.snippet: Backward stable algorithms for eigenproblems running close to matrix multiplication time.
status_evidence.claim: Earlier stability results do not attain O(log(n/δ)) bits of precision.
